• Charlie’s two calm and clinical finishes once again showed why he’s one of the league’s most dangerous forwards
• Just like the reverse fixture earlier in the season, BPR fought their way back into the game after half time

• Charlie Dunkley opened the scoring after being assisted by Jon

data.polishedReport:
Sue's Angels maintained their iron grip on the top of League Ten with a 4-2 victory over BPR FC on Saturday, keeping their perfect record intact with one game remaining in the season. A dominant first-half display, a nerve-testing comeback from the opposition, and a clinical finishing performance in the closing stages ensured the boys stayed on course for what would be a remarkable perfect league campaign—and that's the kind of thing that deserves celebration at this level, where consistency and hunger don't always go hand in hand.

The XI rolled out as follows: Luke Munns in goal, Andrew Allen at left-back, Dean Knight on the right, Jim El Bayati and Richard Epathite in the centre of defence, Kafele Brown and Stewart Luwawa anchoring the midfield, Abiola Adio, Jon Lloyd, and Frazier-Isaías Osunkoya in the three attacking midfield spots, with Charlie Dunkley leading the line. Off the bench came William Clark, Kyrell Mullings, and Samakab Nur.

Sue's Angels came out of the blocks with purpose and put two goals on the board before half-time through the clinical finishing of Charlie Dunkley. Jon Lloyd set up the opening goal with a well-weighted assist, and Dunkley made no mistake—composed, clinical, exactly the kind of finish that has made him one of the league's most dangerous forwards this season. Minutes later, Dunkley struck again, this time on the back of an assist from Frazier-Isaías Osunkoya, doubling the advantage and seemingly putting the match to bed early. Those two calm finishes—the hallmark of a striker in form—gave us a commanding position and set the tone for what we thought would be a fairly straightforward afternoon.

But football, even at Sunday-league level, has a way of humbling you. Echoing the reverse fixture earlier in the season, BPR emerged from the interval with renewed purpose and clawed their way back into the contest. Two quick-fire goals either side of the break hauled them level at 2-2, and suddenly the ground felt the familiar unease of a game slipping away. The déjà vu was palpable—we'd been here before against these opponents, and the pattern threatened to repeat itself. Credit to BPR; they showed character and refused to go quietly. But it's in moments like these that a team's true mettle is tested, and Sue's Angels didn't blink.

The pivotal moment came when Frazier-Isaías Osunkoya, operating in his usual creative role through the middle, won a penalty. Andrew Allen, responding brilliantly to the disappointment of last week's cup final loss, stepped up and restored our lead at 3-2 with a composed conversion. The significance of that goal cannot be overstated—it was the moment that steadied the ship when the waters were choppy, and it sent a message to BPR that we weren't about to fold. Allen's response after that cup final heartbreak showed character and hunger; this is a player who understands what it takes to bounce back.

In the closing stages, Osunkoya added a fourth, driving through the middle with purpose and finishing confidently on his weaker right foot to seal the points. It was a performance that captured everything the 24-year-old midfielder has brought to the side this season: creativity, decisiveness, clinical finishing when it matters. Beyond his two assists, the penalty he won was the catalyst for our comeback, and that's the kind of all-action contribution that wins leagues.

Luke Munns deserves particular mention for a string of high-quality saves in the first half that kept us in control during moments when BPR threatened to ignite. But it was his distribution that caught the eye too—his ball-playing ability off his feet showed another dimension to his game, and in modern football, even at this level, a goalkeeper who can operate in possession is invaluable. Jim El Bayati, our captain, was named Player of the Match, a recognition of his commanding presence at the heart of the defence and his leadership on the pitch.

With one league game remaining and a 100% record intact, Sue's Angels are now within touching distance of something genuinely special. A perfect league season at Sunday-league level is rare—it demands consistency, professionalism, hunger, and the ability to respond when things go wrong. This performance, for all its wobbles, had all of those things. One more push, and we'll have something to be genuinely proud of.

# Sue's Angels Complete Historic Perfect Season With Final Day Victory

The story ended exactly how everyone connected with Sue's Angels FC would have hoped. On a sun-blessed final day at The Reeves Sports Club, we dispatched Hillside Elite FC Blues 2-0 to complete an unthinkable feat: eighteen wins from eighteen league matches. Not a single dropped point. Not a single shared spoil. A perfect season in Division Ten, the first of its kind since the league's inception in 2021/22. When the whistle went, the significance of it all settled in properly. This wasn't just a win. This was history.

The XI that lined up to seal it reflected the blend of consistency and depth we've built: Luke Munns in goal, Andrew Allen at left back, Daniel McLane and Jim El Bayati at centre half—with El Bayati wearing the captain's armband—Dean Knight on the right, and a midfield pairing of Stewart Luwawa and Kafele Brown sitting deep. Elis Brumpton operated centrally ahead of them, while Jon Lloyd and Frazier-Isaías Osunkoya worked the flanks. Alfie James Inman led the line up front. The bench brought Stephen Potter, Jeev Thilaganathan, Samakab Nur, and Michael Brabrook—fresh legs for a day when control of the contest mattered as much as the scoreline itself.

The occasion carried weight beyond our own ambitions. Hillside arrived needing victory to secure promotion, while down the table Brockwell Violets had already finished their season and needed us to do them a favour. The atmosphere crackled with that peculiar tension that comes when promotion, records, and history all converge on ninety minutes of football. Yet we started professionally and controlled large periods of the game, keeping Hillside at arm's length despite the desperation they brought to their task. The opposition remained organised and competitive throughout—you don't reach a promotion position by accident—but we were never really in danger.

Daniel McLane broke the deadlock in the twentieth minute, finishing from a corner kick to open the scoring. It was vintage McLane, really. He's been one of our most dangerous threats from set pieces all season, a menace to defences when the ball swings in from wide, and his instinct to be in the right place at the right moment showed again here. With that early goal, the pressure shifted. Hillside had to chase the game. We could dictate.

The second half saw us put the match beyond doubt when Frazier-Isaías Osunkoya doubled the lead in the 48th minute. The goal came after a superb solo run from Frazier—direct, powerful, exactly the kind of moment that decides matches at this level. Alfie James Inman provided the assist, and with the score at 2-0, the contest was settled. Hillside's promotion hopes withered further when one of their players received a second yellow card and a red, leaving them chasing the result with ten men. The referee managed the occasion well throughout, keeping the focus on the football despite the pressures and significance surrounding everything.

When the final whistle came, we'd done it. Eighteen wins from eighteen. Fifty-four points—a Division Ten record. Ninety goals scored across the league alone. Just eleven conceded. The best defensive record in the division's history. Brockwell Violets got their promotion alongside us as a bonus, which felt right somehow—they'd done their part. Hillside's push fell just short, and you couldn't help but feel for them, but that's the nature of final days.

This is Sue's Angels FC's first season as a club. In thirty-three matches across all competitions, we've scored 137 goals and won eighty-eight per cent of our games. We've reached a cup final, won our league by a margin that speaks to genuine superiority, and claimed promotion at a canter. We're the highest-scoring team across the entire Southern Sunday Football League pyramid. History, records, perfection—it's been an extraordinary debut. And now it's done. The final chapter of an unforgettable first year written exactly as it should have been.

# Match Preview: Sue's Angels FC vs Hillside Elite FC Blues

This is it. The final frame of a story that still feels too good to be true. Sue's Angels FC, a club that didn't exist until this season, have one game left to write themselves into Sunday League folklore—and the script is almost impossibly perfect. One win against Hillside Elite FC Blues on Sunday morning at The Reeves Sports Club will complete something that has never been done in Division Ten's history: an unblemished, 18-game league season. Seventeen wins from seventeen is already the stuff of fantasy. A pristine 18 would be the stuff of legend.

But this fixture carries weight that stretches far beyond our own ambitions. For Hillside, promotion hangs by a thread. They arrive third with 31 points from 17 games, fighting for a place alongside the champions and knowing that anything less than victory will leave them watching others celebrate. Brockwell Violets, sat second with 33 points from their completed campaign, are holding their breath 200 miles away. If we win—when we win—Brockwell make the leap alongside us. If Hillside win, Brockwell's season ends in agonising disappointment. That's the arithmetic of final day. One match carrying three club's seasons in its hands.

Hillside come into this with momentum that shouldn't be dismissed. Four league wins on the spin, 10 goals scored, just 3 conceded. They've found their rhythm at exactly the right moment, and they'll arrive knowing they've got nothing to lose and everything to prove. Context matters, though. We've already beaten them twice. Five-nil away, three-nil at home in the cup semi-final. Those scorelines tell their own story about the gap between the sides. Yet final day football doesn't care about previous results or league positions or historical narratives. Hillside will come to The Reeves with the desperation of a side whose season genuinely depends on the next ninety minutes. That changes everything.

What we need from ourselves is simple but demanding: consistency. Not flash, not showing off, just the same relentless, professional approach that's carried us here. Win first, then chase the records. Those records—the highest points total in Division Ten history (already ours at 51), the defensive record of 14 goals conceded that we could break (we're on 11), pushing toward 90 league goals when we've already netted 88—they'll come if we do the business properly. The 88% win percentage across 32 games in all competitions, the 135 goals scored, the atmosphere this club has built in its first breath of existence: none of that matters if we don't turn up hungry on Sunday morning.

The stakes are genuine but they're also clear-eyed. We've already won the league with four games to spare. We've already broken records. We've already announced ourselves. This isn't about desperation or proving something we haven't already proven. It's about finishing what we started with the standard that got us here. Hillside will fight. They have to. The promotion places are worth fighting for, and they're genuine competitors in strong form. Brockwell will be checking their phones. The records are waiting. But what matters is bringing the same intensity, the same sharpness, the same relentless execution that's carried us through 17 unbeaten.

One win. Ninety minutes on a Sunday morning at the end of May. Unbeaten season, promotion for Brockwell, records broken, history written, and Sue's Angels FC's debut campaign capped with something truly remarkable. It's the kind of thing you dream about as a kid kicking a ball in the park. The fact that it's real, that it's here, that it's minutes away—that's something special. Let's go finish this properly.

Sue's Angels' perfect league record remained intact with a commanding 7-2 victory over Old Freemen's at Meadhurst Sports Club, extending the club's unbeaten run to five wins from five and moving the goal tally to an impressive 28 from their opening five matches. The scoreline tells the story of a team in complete control—dominant, fluid, and finding the net with relentless efficiency. Old Freemen's, despite managing two goals, never posed a serious threat to Sue's Angels' ambitions this season, and the morning's work was a statement of intent from a squad moving through the division with real purpose.

The XI took to the pitch in their familiar 4-2-3-1 shape: Luke Munns between the sticks, Andrew Allen at left-back, Michael Brabrook and Daniel McLane as the centre-back pairing, and Dean Knight on the right flank. Richard Epathite and Stewart Luwawa anchored the midfield, while Stephen Potter, Frazier-Isaías Osunkoya, and Malachi Mullings operated behind Charlie Dunkley in attack. The bench held reinforcements in Jeev Thilaganathan, William Clark, and Abiola Adio. From the first whistle, Sue's Angels looked dangerous throughout the match with constant attacking pressure, and Old Freemen's found themselves under immediate siege.

The goals came with impressive regularity. Frazier-Isaías Osunkoya proved unstoppable, finding the net twice and establishing himself as a central threat in the attacking third. The finishing was clinical when it mattered, with Andrew Allen pulling the strings from left-back and earning two assists before Charlie Dunkley also chipped in with two of his own to fuel the attack. Dean Knight added his name to the scoresheet, profiting from the numerical advantage in the final third, while William Clark made a decisive impact from the bench as a centre-forward, adding another goal to the tally. Daniel McLane, the centre-back, also got among the scorers via a set piece—a reminder of Sue's Angels' threat from dead-ball situations. Stephen Potter contributed a goal of his own amid an otherwise strong team performance that maintained momentum through an impressive opening stretch to the season. Malachi Mullings orchestrated play from his position in midfield, providing crucial assists that underpinned the attacking flow.

What made the afternoon particularly notable was Old Freemen's finally breaching Sue's Angels' previously impenetrable defence. Over the first four league matches, the club had kept four clean sheets, a record that had built a protective wall around the season's early narrative. Old Freemen's forward celebrated wildly when his goal went in—a rare moment of joy for the away side, born partly from the rarity of finding the back of the net against this Sue's Angels defence. The second Old Freemen's goal was an unfortunate own goal from Stephen Potter late in the game, a moment of misfortune rather than any systemic collapse. By that stage, the result was long secured, and such incidents barely registered against the backdrop of Sue's Angels' dominance.

Throughout the match, the boys continued to show their attacking quality and intensity going forward, moving the ball with purpose and creating opportunities with alarming regularity. The attacking pressure never relented, and Old Freemen's never found a comfortable rhythm or a way to genuinely trouble Munns in goal. When substitutions came—Brabrook and Knight withdrawn, Thilaganathan moving to centre-back, Clark introduced at centre-forward, and Adio adding fresh legs on the wing—the pattern of play remained the same. Sue's Angels controlled the game from start to finish and dominated large periods throughout, the sort of performance that justifies a perfect record and speaks to genuine quality within the squad.

Five games, five wins, 28 goals scored, just two conceded. Those numbers don't lie. Sue's Angels have announced themselves as serious contenders in Division Ten, and performances like this—fluid, clinical, and marked by a relentless attacking intent—suggest they'll only tighten their grip as the season deepens. Old Freemen's will have learned a hard lesson about the level required to compete at the top of this division. For Sue's Angels, it's another statement, another three points, another step towards where the ambition of this club is clearly pointing.

# Sue's Angels snatch dramatic cup win at Mala Vida

Sue's Angels FC pulled off a proper smash-and-grab on Saturday, grinding out a 2-1 victory away to Mala Vida FC in the first round of the Marcus Lipton Cup. It was the kind of afternoon that lives in the memory — a performance built on grit, organisation, and the ruthlessness to punish two moments of chaos when they came. The boys go through to the second round, and they've done it against higher-division opposition at that, with half the squad missing through injury and unavailability.

The XI that took to the pitch was a lean, fighting unit, shaped in a 3-5-2 to give us shape and compactness. Luke Munns in goal, with Ross Tomassi, Andrew Allen, Dean Knight, and Sean Sheehan forming a five-man defensive spine across the back. Abiola Adio handled the right-wing-back berth, while Stewart Luwawa, Kafele Brown, and Malachi Mullings occupied the midfield. William Clark and Charlie Dunkley led the line. Jeev Thilaganathan was on the bench, ready if needed.

From the first whistle, Mala Vida showed why they play their football in the divisions above. They moved the ball with a comfort we don't often see on a Sunday morning, worked the pitch with intelligence, and kept possession in a way that announced their pedigree. For large swathes of the first half, we were chasing shadows — but that was the plan, or at least it became the plan. Mala Vida's technical quality meant they carved out chances, and their constant pressure eventually told. A penalty was awarded, and they converted it with the efficiency you'd expect. We went in at half time trailing 1-0, up against it, but still in the game.

The dressing room talk was simple and honest. Stay compact. Stay in it. Wait for our moment. It's unglamorous football, the kind that doesn't fill highlight reels, but it works when you've got the discipline and the nerve to execute it. Mala Vida continued to dominate possession in the second half, continued to pile on the pressure, and Luke Munns began answering the call with save after save — big ones, difficult ones, the kind that keep your team alive when the tide is against you. He was immense, full stop.

Then the game turned. With fifteen minutes to play, a Mala Vida defender headed clear from a corner. The ball fell loose, and Malachi Mullings was there. A volley. Struck with real venom, right underneath the crossbar, and Luke's opposite number was left helpless. One-one. Suddenly we were breathing.

Five minutes later, we took the lead. Will Clark stepped up to a free kick in a dangerous area — he'd already buried one from a set piece against Hillside a fortnight prior, so there was form there. His effort was clean and well-struck, forcing a save, but the goalkeeper spilled it. Mullings was quickest to react, sharp as anything, and tapped home. Two-one. Against the run of play, against the tide of possession, we were ahead.

Mala Vida threw everything at us in those final minutes. The pressure intensified, the home side visibly tired after the physical toll the game had taken on both sides. Luke produced another save that defied belief to keep us in front. The referee wound up and added six minutes of stoppage time, much to the bewilderment of everyone watching, but we stood firm. When it was done, it was done.

This was a cup performance that will be talked about around the club for weeks. Malachi Mullings was our Player of the Match, and rightly so — two goals don't tell the whole story, but they tell enough of it. Andrew Allen, our captain, and the lads around him defended with real bravery against a side that knew what they were doing. Luke kept us in it when we had nothing else. And when the openings came, we buried them without hesitation.

Sue's Angels progress to the second round. That's the story. That's what matters. We'll be back to full strength soon enough, and we'll be ready for whoever comes next.

# Sue's Angels FC 10–1 Sporting Club Catania

There are some victories that don't just win games. They announce something. Sue's Angels FC, in their debut season, secured the Division Ten title in the kind of performance that leaves no doubt about where they belong: on Saturday morning, they dismantled Sporting Club Catania 10–1 at The Reeves Sports Club, and in doing so, mathematically confirmed promotion and the league championship with games still to play. This wasn't a title won by grinding through a tense afternoon. This was a statement. This was a club arriving.

The XI took the field with no hint of the nerves that might reasonably accompany knowing the league title hung in the balance. Luke Munns in goal; Jon Lloyd, Elis Brumpton, Daniel McLane, Jim El Bayati—captain—and Dean Knight across the back line; Andrew Allen and Stewart Luwawa in the middle; Stephen Potter and Frazier-Isaías Osunkoya as support strikers; Charlie Dunkley leading the line. It was a familiar shape, a settled one, and it showed. From the opening whistle, Sue's Angels played with a freedom and a confidence that suggested they'd already accepted the inevitable. The boys delivered something close to football at its most straightforward and most devastating: relentless intensity, attacking quality, and the kind of ruthlessness that comes when a team knows they're better and refuses to apologize for it.

Catania had no answer. Early goals came—Dunkley opened the account, Luwawa adding a second from a set piece with Lloyd providing the assist—and rather than tightening up, rather than managing the lead, Sue's Angels simply continued. This was the point where you could see the gap in class. Potter added a third; Dunkley made it four. The flow didn't stop. Osunkoya—who would run the show all afternoon—made it five before Potter completed his hat trick. It was relentless, and it never felt like overkill because Catania simply couldn't function against what was being asked of them. The intensity never wavered. The movement never stopped. By halftime, the tie was already settled.

The second half produced more of the same. Osunkoya struck again, this time from a set piece, with Kieron Horrill supplying the assist. Dunkley completed his brace to make it eight. Osunkoya finished his hat trick, then Potter rounded off the scoring to make it ten. Each goal came with the kind of ease that only happens when a team is playing at a completely different level. Luke Munns's assist on one of those goals—a goalkeeper's contribution—somehow felt entirely consistent with the evening's trajectory. When you're the best side in the division, everything you do tends to work.

The substitutions told their own story. Jon Lloyd, Daniel McLane, Dean Knight, Stephen Potter, and eventually Charlie Dunkley himself all came off, replaced by Michael Brabrook, Danny Jackson, Kieron Horrill, Samakab Nur, and Jeev Thilaganathan. It was a chance to rest the troops, to rotate, to give squad depth a chance to shine—and Jackson, coming on, provided two assists to prove the bench was ready when called upon.

Frazier-Isaías Osunkoya took Man of the Match, and rightfully so. A hat trick, a constant attacking threat, a dominant display from start to finish. He was everywhere, causing chaos, making the right run, finding the right space. But the truth is that he was operating in a team that moved as one, that understood the assignment, that played with the kind of collective clarity that championship-winning sides display.

This is what it looks like when a club in its first season doesn't just compete for a title but obliterates everyone in their path. Sue's Angels secured promotion and the Division Ten crown in front of their home crowd at The Reeves, and they did it not by defending a lead or grinding out results, but by dismantling every side they faced and, on this particular Saturday, showing Catania exactly why they belong at the top of this division. The trophy presentation comes at the league's end-of-season event, but really, it was already decided here. The boys have announced themselves. And they're not done yet.

data.polishedReport:
# Sue's Angels Fall Short in Dylan Rigobert Trophy Final

The weight of that scoreline — 3-0 — will sit heavy on Sue's Angels FC for a while yet. Not because the defeat stings any less, but because it arrived in circumstances that felt almost cruelly constructed to maximise the sting. On 17 May at Robert Parker Stadium, in the club's first ever cup final, the boys found themselves on the wrong side of fine margins and moments of misfortune that, on another afternoon, might easily have gone the other way.

FC Porto of London take the Dylan Rigobert Trophy home. That's the plain fact. But it doesn't tell the story of how we got there, and this story matters because it shapes what comes next.

The XI rolled out in a 5-2-3: Luke Munns in goal, Michael Brabrook at left wing-back, Alfie James Inman, Daniel McLane and Jim El Bayati across the back, Stewart Luwawa and Andrew Allen in midfield, Jon Lloyd and Frazier-Isaías Osunkoya in the ten spaces, and Stephen Potter leading the line. The bench held Jeev Thilaganathan, Kieron Horrill, Danny Jackson and Samakab Nur — a squad ready to chase the game.

Sue's Angels started with real control. Osunkoya came closest early, crashing a volley from outside the box against the post — a moment that deserved to be a goal and probably felt like one for a fraction of a second. Potter had a couple of good openings too as we built our way into the match, moving the ball with intent and purpose. We were the better side in those opening exchanges. Anyone watching would have had us down as favourites. Then, against the run of play, Porto struck from outside the area. The goal fell like a trap sprung by someone who'd been patient and coldly efficient. Worse followed almost immediately. A quick-fire second, and suddenly we were chasing 2-0 at half time despite large spells of positive play. It's the sort of scoreline that can deflate a dressing room, but our lot came back focused and determined to find a way back into the game.

The second half began with real pressure. We pushed forward looking for the momentum to turn. And we got it — in a crowded corner situation inside the box, a foul was given. Penalty. A lifeline. Andrew Allen stepped up and struck it cleanly, but the Porto keeper had it read. Save. That's a moment. That's a turning point some teams never recover from, because the very next phase of play should have brought us another chance to reset our nerves. Osunkoya drove down the wing moments later, was fouled in the box, and we had a second penalty. Another lifeline. Osunkoya took this one and the keeper saved again. Two massive opportunities squandered in the space of a few minutes. You could feel it draining — the momentum, the energy, the sense that the game might still be ours to win. That's when finals are decided, in those narrow windows where teams can either wrest control back or watch it slip away entirely. We watched ours slip.

With about twenty minutes remaining, while we were still pushing forward looking for that breakthrough, Porto cleared defensively and their winger latched onto the loose ball. He ran through into a one-on-one with Luke, and in that crucial moment our keeper slipped. It was the sort of misfortune that can haunt a player, but Luke had been solid throughout. The ball rolled into an open goal and made it 3-0. That was the match.

Fine margins. Missed opportunities. A moment of simple misfortune. That's the narrative the coach put plainly, and it's an honest one. We created chances — more than enough to win a cup final. We didn't take them. Porto did. That's football. That's Sunday League football, where margins are narrower and luck matters because there's no margin for error.

This is Sue's Angels' first season as a club, and they've reached a cup final. That's not nothing. The lessons here are valuable ones about execution, about converting pressure into goals, about how fine the line is between celebration and heartbreak in knockout football. There's no shame in losing like this — only in the feeling that it could have been different. And that feeling, properly channelled, is exactly what builds sides that come back stronger.

Porto deserved their trophy. They were efficient when it mattered. But both sides will meet again, and next time Sue's Angels will be wiser for this afternoon's experience.

Sue's Angels FC beat Pure Football FC 2.0 2-0 away in a pre-season friendly on Sunday 2 August 2026, at Barn Elms Sports centre, a solid win.

Sue's Angels FC lined up in a 3-4-2-1. Stewart Luwawa wore the armband.

On the scoresheet: Ade Owolona (with his left foot from inside the box) and Leon Burnett (with his right foot from outside the box, sent through by Ade Owolona).

Neither Ade Owolona nor Leon Burnett had started a competitive match for the club before this one. Luke Munns has kept thirteen clean sheets for the club.

Pure Football will be in League Eight with us this season, so it was a useful early look at them. The youngsters were quality at the back alongside Jim.

Jeev impressed in the first half. Stewart was given the armband and looked rusty, understandably in a first pre-season game.

Harry brought that engine in the middle, on the front foot all afternoon, never stopped running. Good to see the boys come off the bench.

Both scorers joined from Sheen Park over the summer. A tough afternoon in the heat, shaking off the rust.

Ade showed signs of quality, with some beautiful touches and passes, and it was his pass that put Leon through for the second. Leon, LJ to the lads, made an impact on his first start.

The clubs have met before: 2 meetings and 2 wins, 12 scored and 1 conceded. The last two finished 5-0 at home in Sep 25 and 7-1 away in Nov 25.

Thanks to Pure Football for hosting and good luck to them for the season.

Line-up: Luke Munns (Goalkeeper), Samakab Nur (Left wing back), Sean Sheehan (Left centre back), Jim El Bayati (Centre back), Sam Nichols (Right centre back), Daniel Thorz (Right wing back), Jeev Thilaganathan (Left defensive midfielder), Stewart Luwawa (Right defensive midfielder), Harry Pyke (Left attacking midfielder), Ade Owolona (Right attacking midfielder), Leon Burnett (Striker).
Shape: 3-4-2-1.
Captain: Stewart Luwawa.
Goals: Ade Owolona, Leon Burnett.
Clean sheet: Luke Munns.
Saves: Luke Munns 6.

data.lede:
Sue's Angels FC bid an emotional farewell to club captain Jim on Sunday as he made the final playing appearance of his football career.

While the occasion marked the end of an era on the pitch, it also provided an opportunity to celebrate the impact one individual has had on the club during its historic first season.

Since the formation of Sue's Angels FC, Jim has been much more than a captain. He has been a leader, a role model and one of the driving forces behind everything the team has achieved.

At the heart of a defence that helped deliver an unbeaten league campaign, Jim's performances throughout the season have been consistently outstanding. Week after week, he led by example, setting standards both on and off the pitch and earning the respect of teammates, opponents and everyone connected with the club.

It seemed only fitting that his final appearance ended in typical fashion. A commanding display, a Man of the Match performance and another clean sheet helped complete a season that will be remembered for years to come.

For manager Stephen Epathite, the moment was particularly emotional.

"Jim is my friend, my brother and someone I respect completely as both a man and a footballer. Everything he has given to this club has been done with honesty, commitment and pride. He has all my love and respect."

While Sue's Angels will undoubtedly miss seeing their captain cross the white line each Sunday, there is good news for everyone associated with the club.

Jim's playing days may be over, but his involvement with Sue's Angels FC is far from finished. He will remain part of the club and join the coaching staff on the sidelines next season as the Angels prepare for life in League Eight.

As one chapter closes, another begins.

Thank you for everything, Jim.

A captain. A leader. A friend. A Sue's Angels legend.
data.title: Jim's Playing Career Comes to an End, But His Sue's Angels Journey Continues

Sue's Angels FC can confirm that William Clark has announced his retirement from football.

William played an important role during the club's historic debut season, helping the Angels secure the Division Ten title and complete an unbeaten league campaign.

Across 17 appearances, William contributed 7 goals and 8 assists, often making an impact from the bench and proving to be a valuable part of the squad throughout the season.

Everyone at Sue's Angels FC would like to thank William for his commitment, contribution and support during his time with the club.

We wish him all the very best for the future and congratulate him on leaving the game as a league champion.

Thank you, William

data.lede:
Following a historic and unforgettable 2025/26 campaign, Sue's Angels FC are proud to announce our End of Season Award winners.

An undefeated league season. Division Ten Champions. A record-breaking defensive campaign. History made.

While football is always a team game, these awards recognise the individuals who made an exceptional contribution to one of the greatest seasons in the club's history.

Top Assister

Charlie Dunkley

Charlie was simply relentless throughout the season.

Leading the line with energy, intelligence and determination, he was a constant threat for opposition defences. Whether running in behind, stretching the game or creating opportunities for those around him, Charlie's selfless play was just as important as his goals.

His ability to bring teammates into the game and provide crucial assists made him one of the driving forces behind our attacking success.

Defensive Record Award

Luke Munns

Every successful team needs a goalkeeper they can rely on.

For Sue's Angels FC, that goalkeeper was Luke Munns.

Time and time again Luke delivered when called upon, providing the calmness, leadership and match-winning saves that every championship-winning side requires. His performances throughout the campaign helped the club achieve a historic defensive record and finish the season with one of the league's strongest backlines.

A fantastic season between the sticks and a fully deserved award.

Goal of the Season

Malachi Mullings

Some goals win games.

Some goals leave people speechless.

Malachi's stunning strike against Mala Vida falls firmly into the second category.

A moment of pure quality and a goal that perfectly captured the confidence and talent he brings to the side. Malachi played a huge role in the club's success before his season was unfortunately cut short through injury.

Everyone at Sue's Angels FC wishes him a full recovery and looks forward to seeing him back in yellow for the 2026/27 campaign.

Top Goalscorer

Fraizer Isaias Osunkoya

Goals. Goals. And more goals.

Fraizer has the rare ability to change a game in an instant. One moment of quality, one touch, one finish, and suddenly the result looks very different.

His movement, composure and eye for goal made him one of the league's most dangerous forwards and a nightmare for defenders throughout the season.

When the team needed a goal, Fraizer was usually the man delivering it.

Clubman of the Year

Jimi El Bayati

Some people leave a mark that goes far beyond football.

Jimi has been a leader, a role model and a fantastic servant to Sue's Angels FC.

As he brings his playing career to a close, he does so having helped build the culture and standards that have driven the club forward. His commitment, positivity and support for everyone around him have made him an invaluable part of the journey.

A champion on the pitch and an even better person off it.

A true club legend.

Players' Player of the Year

Daniel McLane

If you combined the determination of Nemanja Vidic with the leadership of John Terry, you'd get something close to Daniel McLane.

Voted for by his teammates, Dan's impact this season cannot be overstated.

Defensively, he was as solid as a rock. In the opposition box, he became a genuine weapon from set pieces, producing crucial goals at key moments throughout the campaign.

A warrior, a leader and a player who set standards every single week.

Manager's Player of the Year

Dean Knight

Selected by the management team, Dean Knight's award is recognition of a season built on consistency, versatility and continuous improvement.

Week after week Dean grew into his role and became one of the team's most dependable performers.

Whether playing at right-back, right wing-back or even stepping into goal when required, Dean always delivered. His willingness to do whatever was needed for the team embodied everything Sue's Angels FC stands for.

With two clean sheets to his name as an emergency goalkeeper and outstanding performances across multiple positions, Dean's contribution to the undefeated season was immense.

While these awards recognise individual achievements, this season belongs to everyone.

The players. The coaching staff. The volunteers. The supporters. The sponsors. The families who backed the team every step of the way.

Together, we achieved something special.

An undefeated season.

Division Ten Champions.

A place in Sue's Angels FC history forever.

Champions. Invincibles. Together.
data.title: Invincible Season. Outstanding Individuals. Meet Sue's Angels FC's 2025/26 Award Winners.

data.lede:
Promotion earned, the wait is over: Sue's Angels now know exactly who stands between them and a second successive title charge. The club has been confirmed in League Eight for 2026/27, with the new campaign kicking off on Sunday 6 September.

Nine opponents await. The Angels will go head to head with Barnes Stormers, Bristol City (London) Supporters, Brockwell Violets, Haydons Park, Junction Elite, Pure Football, Three Little Birds, TSM Rovers and Tyne & Thames across the season. A step up in division, the same standard demanded, and a bigger stage for everything the club plays for.

Before a ball is kicked in anger, the groundwork begins. Pre-season training starts on Sunday 19 July at The Reeves in Hanworth, then runs every Wednesday from 22 July and every Sunday. New players are welcome at every session, so anyone who fancies pulling on the shirt should come down or drop the club a DM.

Three friendlies are already in the diary to sharpen things up, against Clapham Chiefs, Brentford Town and Galacticos Elect, with dates to be confirmed.

A new league, new faces and the same purpose. What we do echoes in eternity.
data.title: Angels learn League Eight opponents as pre-season kicks off

After captaining the club through its historic debut season, Jim now begins the next chapter of his journey by joining the coaching staff ahead of the 2026/27 campaign.

A leader from the moment the club was formed, Jim played a central role in establishing the standards, culture and identity that helped transform Sue's Angels FC from a new grassroots side into Division Ten Champions. His commitment, professionalism and consistency set the tone for everyone around him, while his performances on the pitch helped guide the team to an unbeaten league season.

Having worked closely with manager Stephen Epathite throughout the club's first year, Jim's transition into coaching is a natural one. The relationship between the pair extends far beyond football, built on trust, respect and a shared vision for what Sue's Angels FC can become.

As captain, Jim was often an extension of the management team on the pitch. His ability to organise, communicate and bring people together made him one of the most influential figures within the squad. Those qualities will now be invaluable from the sidelines.

In this new role, Jim will help support player development, maintain the club's culture and standards, and provide leadership to a squad preparing for the challenges of League Eight football.

While his playing career may have come to an end, his impact on Sue's Angels FC is far from over.

The captain becomes a coach, but his commitment to the club remains exactly the same.
